doc.title: Lorraine Feather interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 22, 2023

title: Her father as a British outsider and the NAACP
summary: She thinks Black musicians trusted him differently as a Briton; he was horrified by American prejudice.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I’m not sure how to phrase this question but I’ll give it a try.
The fact that he was British, correct?

Do you think that some of the African-American musicians thought of him differently even though he’s white but he was British, that maybe he didn’t bring any of the prejudice that was so apparent at that time?

Yeah. That’s a good question, and I believe they did think of him differently for that reason. He was first entranced with jazz when he listened to “West End Blues,” Louis Armstrong — Louis Armstrong’s “West End Blues” in London. And then when he came over to the States and he was able to meet him he was just so bowled over that these people he admired treated him with such friendliness and he was shocked. I don’t know what the situation was at the time in London, but my dad was horrified at the racial prejudice in the States and became active in the NAACP when I was I think in my teens, but it just — it was horrible. And it was such a short time ago, you know? Just awful. So yeah I think that they might have trusted him a little bit more.
